usage: Polite-neutral; said to a server to get their attention
반말, only with a server you're friendly with or a very casual joint
Could you look over here, please?
Fuller, gentler when the staff is busy
Add 사장님 in a small family-run place to sound warm
examples: 여기요!
Excuse me!
The single word, raised slightly, is enough to call a server
여기요, 주문할게요.
Excuse me, we'd like to order.
Chain it straight into your request so the server comes ready
여기요, 물 좀 더 주시겠어요?
Excuse me, could we get some more water?
여기요 opens, then a polite -주시겠어요 request follows
nuance: 여기요 is literally 여기 ('here') + 요 (the politeness particle), so it means 'over here, please' — the standard way to flag down a server in a Korean restaurant by calling out the place rather than the person. It is polite-neutral: fine for any customer to any server, but it is NOT honorific, so to an elderly owner you might soften it to 사장님 or add 좀 봐 주세요. The nearest alternative is 저기요, which is a hair more tentative/polite because 저기 ('over there') feels less direct than the pointed 여기 — many Koreans use them interchangeably, but 저기요 also works to stop a stranger on the street, while 여기요 is almost only for service settings. English speakers wrongly translate 'excuse me' as 실례합니다 here, but 실례합니다 is for apologizing/squeezing past, not for summoning a waiter; calling a server that way sounds oddly stiff. Raising your hand while saying 여기요 is normal and not rude in Korea.

mistakes: Saying 실례합니다 to call a waiter.
실례합니다 means 'pardon me (for the intrusion)' and is used to apologize or pass by, not to summon staff. To call a server, say 여기요 or 저기요.
Adding 씨 or a name and saying 여기요 씨.
여기요 already addresses the situation, not a person; you don't attach 씨. If you want warmth in a small shop, say 사장님 or 이모 (auntie), not 여기요 씨.
Dropping to 여기 with an unfamiliar server.
Bare 여기 is 반말 and can sound abrupt or bossy to a stranger. Keep the 요 — 여기요 — unless the server is clearly a friend.

usage: Polite-neutral; flag a server or stop a stranger
반말, only with friends or to hesitate before speaking
More formal, when approaching a stranger carefully
Stacking 잠시만요 to hold someone briefly
examples: 저기요!
Excuse me!
Said toward a passing server to get them to come
저기요, 여기 주문 받아 주세요.
Excuse me, could you take our order here?
Use it to call staff, then state what you need
저기요, 혹시 자리 있어요?
Excuse me, do you happen to have a table?
At the door; 혹시 softens the question
nuance: 저기요 is 저기 ('over there') + 요, an attention-getter that literally gestures away from the speaker, which makes it feel slightly softer and more tentative than 여기요 — that indirectness is exactly why Koreans reach for it constantly. It is polite-neutral and extremely versatile: it calls a waiter, stops a stranger who dropped something, or opens a question to a clerk. The dividing line from 여기요 is range and directness: 여기요 ('right here') is pointed and almost exclusively for service/seated situations, while 저기요 also works out in the world to address someone you don't know. To raise the formality with a stranger, shift to 저, 실례지만… ('um, pardon me, but…'). The classic English-speaker error is treating 저기요 as literally 'that place over there' and getting confused — in this set phrase it is purely a polite 'excuse me', the location meaning is bleached out. Don't pair it with a name; it stands alone.

mistakes: Reading 저기요 literally as 'over there'.
As a set interjection it just means 'excuse me'; the spatial meaning is gone. 저기 있어요 ('it's over there') is the literal use, but 저기요 to a person means 'excuse me'.
Using 저기요 to apologize for bumping someone.
저기요 gets attention; an apology is 죄송합니다 / 실례합니다. If you stepped on someone's foot, say 죄송합니다, not 저기요.
Dropping to 저기 with a stranger.
저기 alone is 반말 and sounds like 'hey' — too casual for someone you don't know. Keep 저기요 for politeness with strangers and staff.

english: Could I have the menu, please?
usage: Could I have the menu, please?
반말, only to a friend or family at the table
Could you bring the menu, please?
Let me see the menu again
When you want it back to reorder
examples: 메뉴 좀 주세요.
The menu, please.
Said as you sit down or when the server comes
여기요, 메뉴판 좀 주세요.
Excuse me, could we get a menu?
여기요 to call, then ask for 메뉴판 (the physical menu)
저기요, 메뉴 좀 다시 주시겠어요? 더 시킬게요.
Excuse me, could we see the menu again? We'll order more.
Asking it back mid-meal to add dishes
nuance: 메뉴 좀 주세요 is 메뉴 ('menu') + 좀 (softener) + 주세요 (the honorific 'please give'), the bread-and-butter way a customer asks for the menu. The 좀 here is NOT 'a little'; it is a politeness lubricant that turns a bare order into a gentle request, so dropping it (메뉴 주세요) is grammatical but blunter. Note 메뉴 means the menu as a concept/list, while 메뉴판 specifically names the physical board or booklet — both are natural here, with 메뉴판 slightly clearer when you want the object in hand. To go more formal/deferential, swap 주세요 for 주시겠어요? ('would you give…?'), which phrases it as a question and sounds extra courteous. The English-speaker trap is over-translating 'can I get' as 제가 받을 수 있어요? — Korean expresses 'can I have X' simply as 'please give X' with 주세요; the 'can I' is already baked into the polite request. With family at the table you'd drop to 메뉴 좀 줘.

mistakes: Translating 'Can I get the menu?' as 메뉴를 받을 수 있어요?
Korean doesn't phrase customer requests with 'can I get/receive'; it uses 'please give me' — 메뉴 좀 주세요. The literal 받을 수 있어요 sounds like asking about your ability to receive.
Dropping 좀 and saying only 메뉴 주세요 to staff.
It's understandable but blunt. The softener 좀 makes it polite and natural; keep it: 메뉴 좀 주세요.
Using 메뉴판 when you mean the food choices.
메뉴판 is the physical menu board/booklet; 메뉴 can mean the dishes/options. To ask 'what's good on the menu', say 메뉴 추천, not 메뉴판 추천.

usage: Polite; announces you're ready to order
반말, to a friend deciding for the table
Formal 합쇼체, stiffer or upscale settings
Flagging the server to come take it
examples: 주문할게요.
We're ready to order.
Said the moment the server arrives at your table
여기요, 이제 주문할게요.
Excuse me, we'll order now.
이제 ('now') signals you've finished deciding
주문할게요. 김치찌개 둘이요.
We'll order — two kimchi stews, please.
Open with 주문할게요, then list dishes with 둘이요
nuance: 주문할게요 is 주문하다 ('to order', from Sino-Korean 注文) in the -ㄹ게요 form, which announces YOUR OWN intention as a courteous heads-up: 'I'm going to order (now).' That -ㄹ게요 is the natural register a customer uses — polite but not stiff. The dividing line from 주문 좀 받아 주세요 ('please take our order') is direction: 주문할게요 declares what you will do, while 받아 주세요 asks the server to do something (come and take it); use 주문할게요 when the server is already there, and 받아 주세요 to summon them. For upscale or very formal places you can elevate to 주문하겠습니다. The English-speaker error is reaching for 'I would like to order' and producing 주문하고 싶어요 — grammatically 'I want to order', which sounds oddly like expressing a desire rather than doing it; Koreans simply say 주문할게요. Also don't confuse 주문 ('an order of food/goods') with 명령 ('a command') — only 주문 fits a restaurant.

mistakes: Saying 주문하고 싶어요 to order.
That means 'I want to order' and sounds like stating a wish. To actually place the order, announce it with 주문할게요.
Using 시키다 carelessly as 시킬게요 to the server's face.
시키다 ('to order/make someone do') is fine among friends (뭐 시킬까?) but to the server the cleaner verb is 주문하다. Say 주문할게요 to staff.
Over-formalizing every time with 주문하겠습니다.
합쇼체 can sound overly formal in a casual eatery. Default to 주문할게요; reserve 주문하겠습니다 for upscale or business settings.

usage: Polite; pointing at a menu item or dish
반말, to a friend or at a very casual stall
Add 하나 to specify the quantity
examples: 이거 주세요.
This one, please.
Said while pointing at the menu or a photo
이거랑 이거 주세요.
This and this, please.
이거랑 이거 lets you point to two items in a row
저기요, 이거 하나랑 콜라 하나 주세요.
Excuse me, one of these and one cola, please.
Combining 이거 with another item, each marked 하나
nuance: 이거 주세요 is 이거 (the spoken contraction of 이것, 'this thing') + 주세요 ('please give'), the point-and-order workhorse for any item you can indicate. Crucially, 이거 ('this, near me') belongs to a set — 그거 ('that, near you'), 저거 ('that, away from both') — so pick by where the thing is on the menu or table. A subtle but important alternative is 이걸로 주세요 (이거 + -로, 'with/by this'): use 이걸로 when you are CHOOSING among options ('I'll go with this one'), and plain 이거 when you simply want the object itself; menus and cafés very often hear 이걸로. The English-speaker mistake is forcing the object particle and saying 이것을 주세요 in speech — natives contract to 이거 and usually drop the particle. Another is using 이거 for a person; 이거 is for things only, so never point at someone and say 이거. Add 하나/둘 for quantity: 이거 둘 주세요.

mistakes: Saying 이것을 주세요 in conversation.
The full 이것을 is bookish; spoken Korean contracts to 이거 and drops the particle: 이거 주세요. The written form sounds stiff at a table.
Using 이거 when the item is near the server or far away.
이거 is for what's near you. If you're pointing at something across the room, it's 저거; near the listener, 그거. The wrong one confuses which dish you mean.
Confusing 이거 주세요 with 이거 뭐예요.
주세요 orders the item; 뭐예요 only asks what it is. If you want to buy it, say 이거 주세요, not just 이거 뭐예요 (which means 'what is this?').

english: Could I get some water, please?
usage: 반말, to a friend at the table
examples: 물 좀 주세요.
Some water, please.
Said to a passing server; 좀 keeps it polite
여기요, 물 좀 주세요. 그리고 컵도요.
Excuse me, some water please. And cups too.
Chain a second request with 그리고 …도요
저기요, 물 좀 더 주시겠어요? 다 마셨어요.
Excuse me, could we get more water? We've run out.
더 for a refill, with a reason
nuance: 물 좀 주세요 is 물 ('water') + 좀 (politeness softener) + 주세요 ('please give'). In Korea water is normally free and self-serve or brought on request, so this is one of the most-used lines in any eatery. Again 좀 is NOT 'a little' — it cushions the request; 물 주세요 without it is correct but curt. For a refill you insert 더 ('more'): 물 좀 더 주세요. To sound extra polite, especially to an older owner, use 물 좀 주시겠어요? as a question. The English-speaker trap is asking 'can I have water' as a literal ability question (물 마실 수 있어요? = 'am I able to drink water?') — that asks about permission/capacity, not a request; Koreans say 'please give water'. Also, tap vs. bottled rarely needs specifying since restaurant water is just 물; don't over-explain with 수돗물 ('tap water') unless you truly mean it.

mistakes: Asking 물 마실 수 있어요? to request water.
That means 'am I able to drink water?' — a question about permission/ability, not an order. To get water, say 물 좀 주세요.
Saying 물 좀 주세요 expecting it to mean 'a little water'.
좀 is a softener, not a quantity. It doesn't limit the amount; it just makes the request polite. For a small amount, say 조금만.
Forgetting 더 when you want a refill.
물 좀 주세요 asks for water generally; for more of what you already had, add 더: 물 좀 더 주세요. Without 더 the server may think you have none yet.

usage: Natural extension asking for the top dish
examples: 추천 좀 해 주세요.
Could you recommend something?
Hand the choice to the server when unsure
여기 뭐가 맛있어요? 추천 좀 해 주세요.
What's good here? Could you recommend something?
Pair with 뭐가 맛있어요 to invite their pick
처음 왔는데 추천 좀 해 주시겠어요?
It's our first time — could you recommend something?
처음 왔다 ('first visit') makes the ask natural
nuance: 추천 좀 해 주세요 is 추천 ('recommendation', Sino-Korean 推薦) + 좀 (softener) + 해 주세요 ('please do for me'). The 해 주세요 (해 주다 = 'do as a favor') is what makes it a request for the server's help, not just a statement; the 좀 softens it further. It's the polite go-to when you can't decide and want the staff's pick. The nearest alternatives are content questions: 뭐가 맛있어요? ('what's tasty?') and 뭐가 제일 잘 나가요? ('what sells best?') — these ask for specific info, while 추천 좀 해 주세요 invites them to choose for you; the dividing line is that the recommendation request leans on the server's judgment. The English-speaker error is using 추천하다 without 주다 and saying 추천하세요 — that commands the server TO recommend (like ordering them), which is too blunt; the favor verb 해 주세요 keeps it courteous. Also note 추천 is a 하다-noun, so it needs the verb 하다: with the softener it's 추천 좀 해 주세요, and without it the joined 추천해 주세요 — but never 추천 주세요, since you can't 'give' a recommendation directly.

mistakes: Saying 추천하세요 to the server.
Bare 추천하세요 is an imperative ('you, recommend!') and sounds bossy. The polite favor form is 추천 좀 해 주세요, asking them to do it for you.
Saying 추천 주세요 without 하다.
추천 is a 하다-noun; you can't 'give' it directly. It needs the verb 하다 plus the favor 주다: 추천 좀 해 주세요.
Over-literal 'recommend me' as 저를 추천해 주세요.
저를 추천해 주세요 means 'please recommend ME (to someone)'. To get a suggestion, drop the object: 추천 좀 해 주세요, or specify 메뉴 추천.

english: Could you make it not spicy?
usage: Polite; asking the kitchen to reduce heat
반말, to a friend cooking or a casual stall
덜 ('less') when you want some heat, not none
Can it be made not spicy?
examples: 안 맵게 해 주세요.
Make it not spicy, please.
Said right after ordering a spicy dish
저 매운 거 잘 못 먹어서 안 맵게 해 주세요.
I can't handle spicy well, so please make it not spicy.
Give a reason with 잘 못 먹다 ('not good at eating')
혹시 떡볶이 덜 맵게 해 주실 수 있어요?
Could you possibly make the tteokbokki less spicy?
혹시 + 덜 맵게 for a softer, partial request
nuance: 안 맵게 해 주세요 is 안 ('not') + 맵게 (the adverbial form of 맵다 'to be spicy', so 'spicily') + 해 주세요 ('please make it for me'). The -게 turns the adjective into a manner ('in a not-spicy way'), and 해 주다 asks the cook to make it that way as a favor. The key distinction is 안 맵게 ('not spicy at all') vs. 덜 맵게 ('less spicy'): use 덜 when you still want some heat — many English speakers overshoot with 안 and then find the dish bland. Korean 맵다 is an adjective conjugated irregularly (맵다 → 매워요, but 맵게 for the adverb), and a common error is saying 맵지 않게 — which is actually fine and natural too, just longer; 안 맵게 is the crisp spoken default. Another trap is treating 맵다 like a verb and saying 안 매워 주세요 — you need the adverb 맵게 before 해 주세요, not the conjugated 매워. To check feasibility first, ask 안 맵게 돼요?.

structuredNuance.t: 안 맵게 해 주세요 means 'please make it not spicy'. The -게 turns the adjective into a manner ('in a not-spicy way'), and 해 주다 asks the cook to make it that way as a favor. To check feasibility first, ask 안 맵게 돼요?.

Putting the negative on the wrong word: 맵게 안 해 주세요.
맵게 안 해 주세요 oddly negates the whole 'make' action. The natural placement negates 맵다: 안 맵게 해 주세요.

반말, to a friendly stall owner

Can I get this to go?
Asked before ordering, to check it's possible
여기서 먹을 거예요, 아니면 포장돼요?
Will you eat here, or — can I get it to go?
Contrast 먹다 (dine in) with 포장 (take out)
남은 거 포장돼요? 싸 주시겠어요?

Polite; asking to settle the bill
Let me pay / ring it up
반말, to a friendly owner or a friend treating
Announcing it yourself at the counter

Check, please.
Said at the counter or to the server to pay
저기요, 계산해 주세요. 얼마예요?
Excuse me, we'd like to pay. How much is it?
Pair with 얼마예요 to ask the total
다 먹었어요. 계산할게요.
We're done. I'll pay now.
다 먹었다 ('all eaten') signals you're leaving

usage: Polite; each person pays their own

Said at the counter when each pays their share

제 것만 ('just mine') to pay only your portion
같이요, 아니면 따로요? — 따로 계산해 주세요.
Together or separate? — Separately, please.

english: Thank you for the meal (before eating)
usage: I'll eat well / thanks for the meal
Polite but softer, to someone close who treats
반말, to a friend or family who's treating
examples: 잘 먹겠습니다!
Thanks for the food!
Said to the cook/host just before the first bite
엄마, 잘 먹겠습니다.
Mom, thanks for the meal.
To a parent who made or paid for the food
선배님이 사 주신 거니까 잘 먹겠습니다.
Since you're treating, thank you for the meal.
To a senior treating you; 사 주신 거 ('the thing you bought')

The dividing line from 잘 먹었습니다 is tense: 먹겠습니다 (future) before the meal, 먹었습니다 (past) after — mixing them is the classic learner slip. The English-speaker error is staying silent (since English has no pre-meal phrase) or saying 감사합니다 alone — 잘 먹겠습니다 is the expected, almost obligatory line when someone feeds or treats you; skipping it can read as ungrateful. Don't say it about food you bought entirely for yourself with no host present.

반말, to a friend or family

Thanks, that was great!
Said to the host or even the server on the way out
사장님, 잘 먹었습니다.
Thanks for the meal, boss.
To the owner as you leave a restaurant
덕분에 맛있게 잘 먹었습니다.
Thanks to you, it was a wonderful meal.
덕분에 ('thanks to you') when someone treated you

usage: Polite-neutral; asking if refills are free/possible
반말, casual spot with a friendly server
Once confirmed, ask them to refill

Can I get a refill?
Holding up an empty cup or side dish
반찬 리필 돼요?
Can we get more side dishes?
반찬 ('banchan') refills are often free in Korea
여기요, 콜라 리필 돼요? 아니면 추가예요?

추가 ('an add-on/extra charge') checks if it costs more

usage: Polite-neutral; asking staff for the toilet

저기요, 화장실 어디예요? 안에 있어요?

화장실 밖에 있어요, 비밀번호 있어요? — 네, 1234요.

The dividing line: 화장실 어디예요? asks location, while 화장실 좀 쓸게요 ('I'll use the restroom') announces you're going (a heads-up, not a location question) — don't swap them. 변소 is crude and dated. The neutral polite word for a public toilet is 화장실: 화장실 어디예요?

That asks permission ('may I go?'), not location. In a restaurant you don't need permission; ask where it is: 여기 화장실 어디예요?
Saying 어디 이에요 separately.
The copula fuses: 어디 + 예요 → 어디예요. Writing 어디 이에요 is unnatural; say 화장실 어디예요?

usage: What staff ask; you answer with a number
Honorific 분 + 세요, what polite staff say
examples: 몇 명이요? — 두 명이요.
How many? — Two.
The host asks; you answer with the count
몇 분이세요? — 네 명이요.
How many in your party? — Four.
Staff use honorific 분; you reply with 명
저희 세 명인데 자리 있어요?
There are three of us — is there a table?
State your number with 인데, then ask for seating
nuance: 몇 명이요? is 몇 ('how many') + 명 (the counter for people) + 이요 (polite particle), the question staff ask at the door — 'for how many?'. As a customer you mostly ANSWER it, with 숫자 + 명 + 이요: 한 명이요, 두 명이요, 세 명이요. Note the counter 명 is the plain word for counting people, while 분 is its honorific; staff politely ask 몇 분이세요? (using 분 + the honorific copula 세요), but YOU refer to your own group with humble/plain 명, never elevating yourselves with 분. That asymmetry is the key learner point. Native Korean numbers are used with 명 (한, 두, 세, 네…), not Sino-Korean (일, 이, 삼) — a frequent slip. The dividing line from 몇 사람? is register: 명 is the standard counter; 사람 ('person') as a counter sounds blunter and less polite in service. The English-speaker error is answering with Sino-Korean numbers (이 명) or honorifically calling their own party 분 — both sound off. Just say 두 명이요.

mistakes: Counting your own party with the honorific 분.
분 honors others; for your own group use plain 명: 두 명이요. Saying 우리 두 분이요 wrongly elevates yourselves.
Using Sino-Korean numbers with 명.
명 takes native numbers: 한 명, 두 명, 세 명 — not 일 명, 이 명. So 'two people' is 두 명이요, never 이 명이요.
Answering 몇 명이요? with just a bare number.
A bare '둘' can sound abrupt; attach the counter and polite 요: 두 명이요. It's the natural, complete answer.

usage: Polite; flagging a wrong dish gently
반말, to a friend or casual stall
주문하다 instead of 시키다, a touch more formal
examples: 어, 이거 안 시켰는데요?
Oh, we didn't order this?
Gently flagging a dish that arrived by mistake
저기요, 이거 안 시켰는데요. 다른 테이블 거 아니에요?
Excuse me, we didn't order this — isn't it another table's?
Suggesting the likely mix-up politely
저희는 된장찌개 시켰는데요, 이건 김치찌개네요.
We ordered doenjang stew, but this is kimchi stew.
Name what you DID order to clarify the error
nuance: 이거 안 시켰는데요 is 이거 ('this') + 안 ('not') + 시켰- (past of 시키다 'to order') + -는데요, a soft sentence-ender that signals 'just so you know…' and invites the listener to respond. That -는데요 is the politeness engine: it raises the issue gently rather than accusing, so it's the courteous way to flag a kitchen mistake. 시키다 ('to order food/make someone do') is the casual everyday verb here; the slightly more formal 주문하다 also works (이거 주문 안 했는데요). The dividing line from a blunt 이거 안 시켰어요 ('we didn't order this') is tone — the -는데요 version is softer and less confrontational, which matters when correcting staff. The English-speaker error is omitting -는데요 and stating a flat negative, which can sound like an accusation, or misusing 시키다 vs. 주문하다 register. Another trap: don't say 이거 틀렸어요 ('this is wrong/incorrect') — that's for wrong answers, not a mis-delivered dish; for a mix-up, say you didn't order it or name what you did order.

mistakes: Dropping -는데요 and saying flat 이거 안 시켰어요.
The bare negative can sound accusatory. The soft ender -는데요 raises it gently: 이거 안 시켰는데요? lets the server fix it without feeling blamed.
Saying 이거 틀렸어요 for a wrong dish.
틀리다 means 'to be incorrect (like a wrong answer)'. A mis-delivered dish isn't 'wrong' that way; say 이거 안 시켰는데요 or name what you ordered.
Confusing 시키다 with 식히다.
시키다 is 'to order'; 식히다 is 'to cool down (food)'. 이거 식혔는데요 would mean 'I cooled this' — say 시켰- for ordering.
